PG-01 · Foundation

PostgreSQL Architecture

Processes, shared memory, auxiliary workers, PGDATA, and the system catalogs that connect PostgreSQL’s logical view to its physical storage.

Validated on PostgreSQL 18.6
Core idea. PostgreSQL uses a process-oriented architecture. A supervisor process traditionally called the postmaster manages the server, while each client connection gets its own backend process. Those processes cooperate through shared memory and persistent state.

1. The process model

A PostgreSQL instance is not one large server process handling every client internally. The postmaster remains the supervisor, auxiliary processes perform background work, and each client connection is represented by a separate backend OS process.

Client connection→Backend process→Shared memory→PGDATA
TopicPostgreSQLMySQLMongoDB
Client handlingOne backend process per connectionPrimarily thread-based inside mysqldmongod is primarily multi-threaded
Main cacheshared_buffers + OS cacheInnoDB buffer pool + OS/filesystem cacheWiredTiger cache + OS cache
Remember
The client program and the PostgreSQL session are different things. If psql reconnects after a backend failure, your terminal can stay open while the server-side backend PID and all session-local state are new.

2. Observe the architecture

The easiest way to understand the model is to compare PostgreSQL’s own statistics view with the operating system process list.

PostgreSQL session
SELECT version();
SHOW data_directory;
SHOW shared_buffers;
SHOW io_method;
SHOW io_workers;
SELECT pg_backend_pid();
PostgreSQL 18.6 ...
data_directory
------------------------
/var/lib/pgsql/18/data

shared_buffers
--------------
128MB

io_method
---------
worker

io_workers
----------
3

pg_backend_pid
--------------
5710

Now inspect the server processes from SQL:

SELECT pid, backend_type, datname, usename, state,
       wait_event_type, wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity
ORDER BY pid;
 pid  | backend_type                 | datname  | state
------+------------------------------+----------+--------
 5541 | io worker                    |          |
 5542 | io worker                    |          |
 5543 | io worker                    |          |
 5544 | checkpointer                 |          |
 5545 | background writer            |          |
 5547 | walwriter                    |          |
 5548 | autovacuum launcher          |          |
 5549 | logical replication launcher | postgres |
 5710 | client backend               | postgres | active
Operating system
$ ps -ef | grep '[p]ostgres'

postgres  5539  ... postgres -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/
postgres  5541  ... postgres: io worker 0
postgres  5544  ... postgres: checkpointer
postgres  5545  ... postgres: background writer
postgres  5547  ... postgres: walwriter
postgres  5548  ... postgres: autovacuum launcher
postgres  5549  ... postgres: logical replication launcher
postgres  5710  ... postgres: postgres postgres [local] idle
What this proves
The backend shown by pg_stat_activity is also a real operating-system process. Opening another connection creates another backend PID; closing that connection removes it.

3. Abnormal death vs clean termination

This is where PostgreSQL’s shared-memory design becomes operationally important.

Experiment A — SIGKILL

$ kill -9 5710

The client sees the connection disappear:

server closed the connection unexpectedly
The connection to the server was lost.
Attempting reset: Succeeded.

The postmaster itself remains alive, but PostgreSQL recreates its sibling server processes. In the lab, auxiliary PIDs changed from the 554x range to new PIDs:

postgres  5539  ... postgres -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/
postgres  5803  ... postgres: io worker 0
postgres  5807  ... postgres: checkpointer
postgres  5808  ... postgres: background writer
postgres  5809  ... postgres: walwriter
postgres  5810  ... postgres: autovacuum launcher
postgres  5811  ... postgres: logical replication launcher
SELECT pg_postmaster_start_time();
2026-09-17 08:34:21.567176+00
Why PostgreSQL reacts this way
A backend killed with SIGKILL disappears without cleanup. PostgreSQL cannot safely assume shared state was left consistent, so it treats the event as a crash of a server process and reinitializes the affected server state before continuing.

Experiment B — SIGTERM

$ kill -TERM <backend_pid>

Or, from PostgreSQL:

SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);
Clean termination
Only the selected backend exits. The background process PIDs stay alive.
DBA habit
Prefer PostgreSQL’s session-control functions or a clean SIGTERM. Do not use kill -9 as a normal way to disconnect a session.

4. PGDATA and system catalogs

PGDATA is the cluster data directory. It contains PostgreSQL’s persistent state: per-database files, cluster-wide relations, WAL, transaction metadata, configuration, and other internal structures.

SHOW data_directory;
/var/lib/pgsql/18/data

A useful first mapping is:

PGDATA/
├── base/      # per-database directories
├── global/    # cluster-wide relations
├── pg_wal/    # WAL
└── ...

PostgreSQL’s metadata is stored in regular relational tables called system catalogs. Two useful examples are pg_database and pg_class.

SELECT oid, datname
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY oid;
 oid | datname
-----+-----------
   1 | template1
   4 | template0
   5 | postgres
SELECT c.relname, c.relisshared, pg_relation_filepath(c.oid)
FROM pg_class c
WHERE c.relname IN ('pg_database','pg_class');
 relname    | relisshared | pg_relation_filepath
------------+-------------+---------------------
 pg_class   | f           | base/5/1259
 pg_database| t           | global/1262
Read the paths, not the numbers
The important lesson is not that pg_class happened to be file 1259. It is that a database-local catalog maps under base/<database_oid>/, while a shared catalog such as pg_database maps under global/.

5. Key takeaways

1 connection = 1 backend process.
The backend is a real OS process, not merely an internal thread.
Processes cooperate through shared memory.
That shared state is why abrupt process death matters.
The postmaster supervises the server.
It can survive while sibling server processes are reinitialized.
PGDATA connects logic to disk.
System catalogs describe logical objects; storage paths show where their physical state lives.
